title: Psychology & Counseling
tagline: From psychology foundations to licensed practice — counseling, social work, and psychology paths compared.
summary: Mental-health careers are among the most purposeful — and most regulated. This roadmap maps the real decision tree: psychology foundations in undergrad, the graduate-track fork (counseling/MSW/MFT/school counseling vs PhD/PsyD), supervised practice hours, state licensure, and the therapeutic skills and ethics that define competent practice.

NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: The helping professions — counseling, psychology, social work, marriage and family therapy, school counseling — all treat mental health and wellbeing but differ in training, licensure, settings, and scope.
detail.why: Choosing between them is the most consequential fork on this map; each requires a different graduate degree and leads to different licenses and daily work.
learn: Read the BLS profiles for counselors, psychologists, and social workers
List what each profession is licensed to do in your state
Note typical degree length and cost for each path
Follow practitioners from 3 professions for a month

resources.title: BLS OOH — Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and Mental Health Counselors

detail.description: In broad strokes: counselors (LPC/LMHC) do talk therapy with master's-level training; clinical social workers (LCSW) blend therapy with case management and systems navigation; psychologists (PhD/PsyD) add assessment, research, and testing; MFTs specialize in relational/systemic therapy.
detail.why: The work overlaps more than people expect — but training model, assessment authority, and insurance reimbursement differ, and they shape your career options.
learn: Compare the 4 licenses: education, hours, exams, scope
Identify which professions can do psychological testing (psychologists, typically)
Note settings where each dominates (schools, hospitals, private practice)
Talk to one licensed professional from two different professions

detail.description: Mental-health professionals work in outpatient clinics, hospitals, schools, universities, private practice, community agencies, correctional settings, employee assistance programs, and telehealth platforms.
detail.why: Setting determines caseload, population, schedule, paperwork, and burnout risk — often more than the license itself does.
learn: List 6 settings and one pro/con of each
Note which settings require evenings/weekends (community MH often does)
Compare agency employment vs private practice economics
Pick 2 settings to observe via volunteering

resources.title: BLS OOH — Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and Mental Health Counselors

detail.description: Clinical work demands emotional regulation, boundaries, comfort with distress, and self-reflection — plus tolerance for years of training before independent practice.
detail.why: Programs screen for readiness, and your future clients deserve clinicians who have done their own work. Honest self-assessment now prevents costly attrition later.
learn: Reflect on your own experiences with counseling or support roles
Practice sitting with someone's distress without fixing it
Assess your financial runway for 2–6 years of training
Consider personal therapy — many programs expect it

detail.description: A psychology bachelor's is the standard on-ramp (though related majors like social work or human services also work): intro psychology, research exposure, and electives aligned to your track.
detail.why: Graduate admissions weigh GPA, research exposure, relevant experience, and fit — the bachelor's years are where you build all four.
learn: Maintain the GPA target your dream programs list
Choose electives deliberately: abnormal, developmental, social
Join a professor's research lab early
Keep a running experiences log for applications

detail.description: The core curriculum — biological bases, cognition, learning, social psychology, personality theory — gives you the vocabulary and models every clinical training builds on.
detail.why: Graduate programs assume this base; admissions committees read transcripts for it.
learn: Study the major perspectives: biological, behavioral, cognitive, humanistic, systemic
Summarize one classic study from five subfields
Connect theories to what you observe in people
Explain one theory to a non-psychology friend

detail.description: Research methods and statistics are the most underestimated prerequisite: study design, validity, reliability, and basic inferential statistics. Every accredited program requires them.
detail.why: Evidence-based practice means reading research critically — and methods courses are the most common GPA risk on transcripts.
learn: Learn to read a journal article's methods and results sections
Understand basic tests: t-test, correlation, ANOVA concepts
Evaluate one pop-psychology claim against real evidence
Take the course seriously — it signals rigor to admissions

detail.description: Abnormal psychology surveys major conditions (mood, anxiety, psychosis, substance use) and lifespan development traces change from childhood through aging — the two content pillars of clinical training.
detail.why: These courses confirm your interest and shape your population preference (children, adults, older adults) — which drives program choice.
learn: Learn major diagnostic categories at a survey level
Study attachment and developmental milestones basics
Note the difference between describing and diagnosing (diagnosis is for clinicians)
Identify which populations energize you

detail.description: Crisis-line volunteering (hotlines, text lines, warming centers) provides real contact with people in distress, structured listening training, and supervised support — the most valued pre-graduate experience.
detail.why: Admissions committees read it as evidence of both commitment and aptitude; you learn whether the emotional workload suits you.
learn: Complete a crisis-line training program
Take shifts weekly for a semester minimum
Practice reflective listening verbatim in your log
Debrief difficult calls with supervisors

detail.description: Graduate options: master's in counseling (2 yrs), MSW (2 yrs), MFT master's (2 yrs), school counseling master's, or doctoral programs (PhD/PsyD, 5–7 yrs). Admission weighs GPA, experience, essays, and fit with faculty.
detail.why: This is the largest financial and temporal commitment on the map — understanding the full menu before applying protects you from the wrong fork.
learn: Compare cost and length across the four master's tracks
Understand accreditation (CACREP, CSWE, COAMFTE, APA) before applying
Draft your application narrative from your experience log
Request letters from supervisors who've seen clinical-adjacent work

detail.description: A master's in clinical mental health counseling trains counselors in theory, ethics, assessment, and supervised practice — leading to state licensure as LPC, LMHC, or equivalent (titles vary by state).
detail.why: Counseling is the most direct route to doing talk therapy as a career, with strong demand and clear licensure steps.
learn: Verify CACREP accreditation of any program you consider
Study the eight core counseling areas the curriculum covers
Understand your state's license title and requirements
Compare program clinical-placement quality, not just cost

detail.description: CACREP (Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs) is counseling's programmatic accreditor. Many states' licensure boards and the NBCC gateway align with CACREP standards.
detail.why: Choosing a CACREP-accredited program protects licensure portability and exam eligibility — one of the highest-leverage decisions on this map.
learn: Search CACREP's directory before shortlisting programs
Understand how CACREP aligns with your state board's rules
Note what happens with non-accredited programs in your state
Ask programs about licensure pass rates

resources.title: NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: The Master of Social Work leads to licensed clinical social work (LCSW after supervised hours and exam): therapy plus case management, advocacy, and systems work across hospitals, schools, agencies, and private practice.
detail.why: MSW is the most flexible mental-health degree — the LCSW license is accepted nearly everywhere and social work spans macro, mezzo, and micro practice.
learn: Verify CSWE accreditation for MSW programs
Compare clinical vs macro MSW concentrations
Understand the LCSW steps in your state (hours + ASWB exam)
Note MSW programs value diverse backgrounds — not only psych majors

resources.title: O*NET — Child, Family, and School Social Workers

detail.description: Marriage and family therapists train in systemic and relational therapy — treating couples, families, and individuals in relationship context. Licensure (LMFT) requires a COAMFTE-accredited or equivalent master's, supervised hours, and an exam.
detail.why: MFT is the profession of choice for relationship-centered work and one of the fastest-growing licenses.
learn: Compare systemic vs individual therapy models
Verify COAMFTE accreditation or state equivalency
Understand LMFT hour requirements in your state
Practice genograms and systemic case conceptualization

resources.title: BLS OOH — Marriage and Family Therapists

detail.description: School counselors support students' academic, career, and social-emotional development across whole schools — classroom lessons, short-term counseling, college/career guidance, and crisis response — under state school-counselor certification.
detail.why: A distinct license from clinical counseling, with school-calendar schedules and growing demand; O*NET tracks it as educational, guidance, and career counselors.
learn: Check your state's school counselor certification route
Compare ASCA National Model concepts (the professional framework)
Note the difference from school psychologists (assessment-heavy)
Observe a school counselor's week if possible

resources.title: O*NET — Educational, Guidance, and Career Counselors

detail.description: Psychologist licensure requires a doctoral degree: PhD (research-emphasis, often funded) or PsyD (practice-emphasis, often tuition-heavy), followed by a year-long internship and postdoctoral supervised experience, then the EPPP exam and state license.
detail.why: Psychologists can conduct psychological testing/assessment and hold the field's doctoral-level roles — but the training is 5–7+ years and admissions to funded programs are very competitive.
learn: Compare PhD vs PsyD funding models honestly
Research APA-accredited programs (required for licensure in many states)
Build research experience — it's the currency of PhD admissions
Talk to 3 psychologists about whether the doctorate was worth it

detail.description: A decision frame: counseling (therapy-focused, efficient), MSW/LCSW (most portable, systems-spanning), MFT (relational focus), school counseling (youth, school calendar), psychology doctorate (assessment, research, academia).
detail.why: All five lead to meaningful practice. The 'best' is the one matching your population, setting, timeline, and finances.
learn: Score each track on your top 5 criteria (time, cost, setting, scope, portability)
Interview one graduate of each track you're considering
Check licensure recognition if you may move states/countries
Commit — and write down why for future doubting days

detail.description: Graduate clinical training includes practicum (early, limited caseloads) and internship (a substantial supervised placement) — your first real clients, under weekly supervision.
detail.why: This is where competence is actually built. Sites with strong supervision teach more than prestigious ones with weak oversight.
learn: Interview potential sites about supervision structure
Treat supervision as the main course — prepare cases for it
Keep a caseload log with presenting issues and modalities
Request letters while your supervisors know your work

detail.description: Post-graduate licensure requires supervised clinical experience — commonly in the low thousands of direct-client hours over roughly two years, with weekly supervision. Exact totals vary by state and license.
detail.why: Hours are the bridge between graduation and independent practice; planning the earning of them (site, pay, supervision quality) is a career decision in itself.
learn: Read your state board's exact hour requirements and supervision rules
Compare associate-level job sites: pay, client volume, supervision
Track hours meticulously from day one
Know what counts (direct vs indirect) before you start

resources.title: NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: Clinical ethics covers confidentiality and its limits (danger to self/others, abuse reporting), informed consent, dual relationships, scope of practice, and mandated-reporting duties — tested at licensure and used daily.
detail.why: Ethical practice protects clients and your license. Most disciplinary cases trace to ethics, not skill.
learn: Learn confidentiality and its legal exceptions cold
Understand informed consent elements for therapy
Study dual/multiple relationships in small communities
Know your state's mandated-reporting thresholds

detail.description: Clinical documentation — intake assessments, treatment plans, progress notes (SOAP/DAP), and outcome measures — is both clinical tooling and legal/insurance record.
detail.why: Documentation quality drives reimbursement, continuity of care, and legal safety; supervisors evaluate it heavily.
learn: Write a DAP note for 5 mock sessions
Draft a measurable treatment plan with objectives and interventions
Understand medical-necessity language for insurance
Practice concise, objective, non-judgmental note style

resources.title: BLS OOH — Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and Mental Health Counselors

detail.description: Evidence-based modalities — CBT (cognitive-behavioral), DBT-informed work, motivational interviewing, trauma-informed approaches, solution-focused brief therapy — each carry models, manuals, and training paths.
detail.why: Employers and payers increasingly specify modality training; your theoretical home shapes supervision, jobs, and results.
learn: Study CBT fundamentals: thoughts-feelings-behaviors, homework, structure
Learn motivational interviewing's spirit and core skills (OARS)
Understand what trauma-informed care means in practice
Sample one session script from each of three modalities

detail.description: Licensure is state-specific: LPC/LMHC for counselors, LCSW for clinical social workers, LMFT for family therapists, psychologist licenses for doctoral clinicians — each with its board, application, hours verification, and exam.
detail.why: The license is the profession's gateway to independent practice and insurance panels. Application timing and documentation determine how fast you get there.
learn: Bookmark your state board's licensure page
Collect hour logs and supervisor forms as you go
Understand associate/provisional license titles while accruing hours
Check endorsement rules if you might move states

certs.name: LPC / LMHC
certs.note: Typically requires a CACREP-aligned master's, supervised post-degree clinical hours (varies by state, commonly ~2,000–4,000), and a licensing exam.

resources.title: NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: Licensure exams by profession: NCE (National Counselor Examination, via NBCC) and NCMHCE for counselors; ASWB exams for social work; AMFTRB exam for MFTs; EPPP (ASPPB) for psychologists.
detail.why: Exams gate the license; structured 8–12 week preparation with practice exams is the standard successful approach.
learn: Identify your profession's exam and its structure
Build a study calendar with a commercial or official prep source
Take full-length practice exams under timing
Schedule the exam for your strongest prep window

resources.title: NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: For social workers: MSW → supervised clinical experience → ASWB clinical exam → LCSW. For MFTs: master's → supervised hours → AMFTRB exam → LMFT. Titles and hour thresholds vary by state.
detail.why: Both licenses open independent therapy practice; knowing the exact sequence prevents gap-year surprises.
learn: Map the LCSW steps in your state precisely
Map the LMFT steps if that's your track
Compare supervision costs across states
Plan income during the supervised-years phase

detail.description: Licensed clinicians branch: agency clinician → supervisor/clinical director; private practice owner; school or university counselor; program management; training and supervision; forensic, health-psych, or policy-adjacent roles.
detail.why: Licensure is a platform, not a destination. Supervision credentials (e.g., approved supervisor status) and niche expertise compound into senior roles.
learn: Map 3 career destinations with realistic timelines
Identify which specialization your practicum population suggests
Join your professional association early (students get discounts)
Set a 5-year sketch including supervision aspirations

resources.title: BLS OOH — Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and Mental Health Counselors

detail.description: Private practice means running a small business: licensure and insurance panels, EHR and billing, a niche, referral streams, fees, and boundaries — typically after some agency years.
detail.why: Private practice offers autonomy and is the most common long-term destination — but clinicians who plan the business side thrive while others burn out.
learn: Learn insurance paneling basics (or choose cash-pay deliberately)
Understand record-keeping, HIPAA-compliant tools, and billing
Define a niche and referral sources
Model caseload economics before leaving salaried work

resources.title: BLS OOH — Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and Mental Health Counselors

detail.description: Teletherapy is now standard: platform-based sessions, digital intake and consent, crisis protocols at a distance, and licensure considerations across state lines.
detail.why: Telehealth expanded access and job options dramatically — including platforms, group practices, and location-flexible careers.
learn: Practice teletherapy presence (camera framing, pacing, silence handling)
Learn emergency protocols for remote clients (location, contacts)
Understand interstate licensure limits (PSYPACT-style compacts exist for psychologists)
Compare platform employment vs independent telehealth

detail.description: Licenses require ongoing continuing-education hours per renewal cycle, plus optional advanced trainings and certifications in modalities (trauma work, addictions, supervision) that deepen practice.
detail.why: CE is both a legal requirement and your main lever for specialization and rate increases.
learn: Note your license's CE cycle and approved providers
Choose CE that builds a coherent specialization, not random credits
Track certificates from day one
Explore supervision training as a CE investment

resources.title: NBCC — National Board for Certified Counselors

detail.description: Vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue, and burnout are occupational risks of clinical work. Sustainable practice rests on caseload realism, supervision, peer consultation, personal therapy, and life outside work.
detail.why: Burnt-out clinicians harm clients. Building sustainability habits during training protects both you and the people you serve.
learn: Learn the signs of compassion fatigue and vicarious trauma
Set a sustainable caseload number and defend it
Join or form a peer consultation group
Keep personal therapy in your routine — it's the field norm

detail.description: Clinicians practice within defined scope — diagnosis and treatment within their license — and many extend into advocacy: community mental health, policy participation, and reducing access barriers.
detail.why: Scope discipline protects clients and licenses; advocacy extends impact beyond the therapy room and defines the profession's public role.
learn: Review your scope-of-practice rules and referrals
Learn how licensure boards handle scope complaints
Follow your professional association's advocacy work
Volunteer for one community mental-health initiative
